title: TypeScript Discriminated Unions & Exhaustiveness Checking
description: Master control-flow analysis, the satisfies operator, and compile-time exhaustiveness guarantees in TypeScript.
author: Qodlume Editorial

questions.prompt: Why is the 'satisfies' operator preferred over a colon type annotation (: Record<string, string | number>) in the configuration below?

options.text: satisfies validates compatibility with the target type without widening property types, preserving string methods on palette.primary.
satisfies freezes the object at runtime like Object.freeze().
satisfies strips extra properties at compile time.
satisfies converts numeric literals to strings automatically.

questions.explanation: A standard type annotation (: Record<string, string | number>) widens every property value to string | number, making palette.primary.toUpperCase() a compile error. The satisfies operator checks structural conformance while keeping the narrow inferred type for each property.

references.title: TypeScript 4.9 Release Notes: The satisfies Operator

questions.prompt: Which TypeScript type represents an unreachable code path and is idiomatically used in the default branch of a switch statement to enforce exhaustiveness?
questions.explanation: The 'never' type represents the empty set of values. When all union members are handled in prior case clauses, control-flow analysis narrows status to 'never'. If a new member is later added to Status, assigning status to 'never' fails at compile time.

questions.prompt: What is the effect of 'noUncheckedIndexedAccess: true' in tsconfig.json when indexing into a Record<string, Quiz>?

options.text: It throws a runtime RangeError when a key is missing.
It appends '| undefined' to the indexed access type (Quiz | undefined), forcing callers to guard against missing keys.
It disallows bracket notation on objects entirely.
It converts all Record types into Map instances during compilation.

questions.explanation: Enabling noUncheckedIndexedAccess includes 'undefined' in the type of any index signature lookup, preventing unsafe assumptions that arbitrary dictionary keys or array indices always exist.
